100.title: Red flag screening: shoulder or neck symptoms

redFlags.text: Gait disturbance, including unstable or unsteady gait, gait instability, or new-onset gait imbalance
Bowel or bladder changes, including bladder or bowel incontinence, urinary urgency, or bladder dysfunction
Loss of hand dexterity or hand clumsiness
Severe, unrelenting pain despite guideline-directed treatment
Radicular symptoms associated with a traumatic injury
Pain over the clavicle shaft: an occult or stress fracture must always be ruled out, even in the absence of trauma and especially in elderly people
Diminished radial pulse, with positional pain worse with neck extension and shoulder abduction, extension, and external rotation
Positional paresthesias exacerbated by overhead activity with associated vascular signs
Paresthesia and weakness in intrinsic hand muscles due to compression of the brachial plexus, with ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis (Horner's syndrome), as in Pancoast syndrome
Involvement of multiple root levels, especially following trauma
Cancer history or suspicion of malignancy
Recent severe fall or acute trauma
Acute localized bony tenderness over spine or shoulder complex

200.title: Differential: cervical provocative tests
200.questionText: Perform the Spurling test (axial compression while extending and rotating the neck toward the symptomatic side; sensitivity 30-50%, specificity 74-93%) and the Arm Squeeze test (sensitivity 96%, specificity 90%). Is either test positive? Both are strongly indicative of cervical radiculopathy.

options.label: Spurling test positive and/or Arm Squeeze test positive
Both tests negative (Spurling sensitivity is only moderate, so a negative test does not exclude radiculopathy)

210.title: Differential: pain radiation
210.questionText: Where does the pain localize and radiate? Intrinsic shoulder pain most commonly localizes to the lateral deltoid region, the acromioclavicular joint, and/or the biceps tendon and bicipital groove. Cervical radiculopathy presents with arm pain originating from the neck and radiating beyond the elbow, with motor and sensory deficits.

options.label: Pain originates from the neck and radiates beyond the elbow, with motor and sensory deficits
Pain localized to the lateral deltoid region, acromioclavicular joint, or biceps tendon and bicipital groove, without radiation beyond the elbow

220.title: Differential: night pain
220.questionText: Is nocturnal pain or sleep disturbance present? Nocturnal pain is highly indicative of shoulder pathology (almost 90% of patients with symptomatic rotator cuff tears report nocturnal pain and generalized sleep disturbance). Nocturnal pain is not highly indicative of cervical spine pathology.

options.label: Nocturnal pain or sleep disturbance present

300.title: C-spine origin favored
300.primaryDiagnosis: Findings favor cervical spine origin (cervical radiculopathy).
differentials: Shoulder pathology (rotator cuff tear, impingement, glenohumeral arthritis)

400.title: Shoulder origin favored
400.primaryDiagnosis: Findings favor intrinsic shoulder origin (for example rotator cuff disease).

500.title: Origin indeterminate
500.primaryDiagnosis: Neither cervical nor shoulder criteria are met. The source of symptoms is indeterminate, and cervical and shoulder pathology may coexist.

999.title: Emergency referral
999.primaryDiagnosis: Emergency referral: a positive red flag requires prompt evaluation and specialist referral. Possible causes include cervical myelopathy, progressive neurologic deficit, spinal cord compression, infection, neoplasm (including Pancoast tumor), fracture, or vascular compromise.
